chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from al-Abbas ibn Hilal, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

It was mentioned that Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah entered the Sacred Mosque and came to Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him). He said to them, 'By what do you judge?' They said, 'By the Book of Allah and the Sunnah.' He said, 'And what do you do with what you do not find in the Book and the Sunnah?' They said, 'We exert our own opinion (ijtihad ra'yuna).' He said, 'Your own opinion? What do you say about a woman and her female slave who were nursing two boys in a house, and a roof collapsed on them, killing them, while the two boys survived?' They said, 'The Qafi (a specific share/ruling).' He said, 'The Qafi is one who is given a stern look (or is deemed sufficient) for them.' They said, 'Then inform us.' He said, 'No (it is not the Qafi).'

Ibn Dawud said, 'My ransom be for you, it reached me that Amir al-Mu'minin Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no group of people who delegated their affair to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and cast their lots, except that the most accurate lot emerges.' So he fell silent.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful), title for Imam Ali (AS)
key_terms.ابن أبي ليل: Ibn Abi Layla, a prominent early jurist
key_terms.ابن شبرمة: Ibn Shubrumah, a companion of the jurists
key_terms.الْقَافَةَ: Al-Qafi, a specific term in inheritance law referring to a share or a specific ruling
key_terms.نَجْتَهِدُ رَأْيَنَا: We exert our opinion (Ijtihad bi al-Ra'y)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on inheritance when a mother and her slave die leaving two sons, according to Ibn Abi Layla and Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the transition from subjective juristic opinion (ra'y) to established precedent, as Imam al-Rida (AS) corrects Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubruma by citing a specific ruling from Imam Ali (AS) regarding the inheritance of a mother and her slave who die simultaneously. The dialogue highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precision of legal deduction, where the 'Qafi' (equal share) is determined not merely by logic but by authoritative tradition, reinforcing the concept of divine justice in inheritance distribution. The concluding remark by Ibn Dawud underscores the reliability of the Imams' judgments when they delegate authority to God, a key theme in Shia jurisprudence.
